n: In this lecture we will study alkyl halides. The outline: chloroform, chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride and dichloroethane — their toxicological significance, metabolism, and methods of qualitative and quantitative determination. Key terms: toxicological significance, object, steam distillation, chloroform, chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride, dichloroethane and distillate. The analysis plan consists of two parts: general reactions, that is, organically bound chlorine, isonitrile, Fehling, resorcinol, Fujiwara, and the reactions specific to each substance.

t: Alkyl Halides in the Group of Volatile Poisons
n: Alkyl halides belong to the group of volatile poisons. Among the 13 volatile poisons tested for in a full analysis are chloroform, chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride and dichloroethane. Their formulae: chloroform CHCl3, chloral hydrate CCl3CHO · H2O, carbon tetrachloride CCl4, 1,2-dichloroethane CH2Cl–CH2Cl. Distillation methods are used to isolate these substances from a biological object. To distinguish chloroform and chloral hydrate, an ether extract is obtained from the distillate in pure form.

Azeotropes and steam distillation. Chloroform and water form an azeotrope, that is, a mixture that boils without separating; the composition of its distillate does not change. The amount of water in the azeotrope, in percent by weight: with chloroform 2.5%, with carbon tetrachloride 4.1%. The azeotrope of 1,2-dichloroethane and water boils at 71.62 °C, and the water in it is 8.2%. Azeotropes can be separated by simple or fractional distillation, or by a chemical method.

Now chloroform. Chloroform, CHCl3, is a compound that has a toxic effect on the body. In the national economy it is used for dissolving paints, removing stains from clothing, and extracting medicinal compounds from plants. It is also used as an anaesthetic in surgical operations. Formerly it was used as an anaesthetic; by its pharmacological action it belongs to the group of narcotic substances.

Chloroform poisoning is possible through the respiratory tract and the stomach. 5-10 g of chloroform leads to severe poisoning. Symptoms such as severe pain in the stomach and nausea are felt. Death occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre. The pathological-anatomical picture is not characteristic, that is, there are no specific signs in the corpse.

t: Chronic Poisoning and Signs in the Corpse
n: In chronic poisoning, liver function fails and cirrhosis of the liver develops. The kidneys and the heart muscle also fail. After entering the body, chloroform accumulates in fatty tissue. In some cases a characteristic smell of chloroform may come from the corpse.

Chloroform metabolism. It is eliminated from the body unchanged. 30-50% of CHCl3 is eliminated unchanged through the respiratory tract within 15-20 minutes, and 90% after an hour. The remainder undergoes biotransformation. Even after 8 hours, a residue of CHCl3 can be determined in the blood. In part it is oxidised to CO2 and HCl.

Physical properties of chloroform. It is a colourless, clear, mobile liquid, considerably heavier than water and poorly soluble in it, in the ratio of 1:200. It evaporates in open air; it has a specific characteristic odour, and a sweetish, unpleasant taste. It mixes well with ether and other organic solvents. It distils quickly and easily with steam. Its boiling point is 61.16 °C.

Chloroform and phosgene. In open air, under the action of sunlight, chloroform is oxidised to form a very poisonous compound, phosgene. The reaction: CHCl3 + O → COCl2 + HCl; the structure of phosgene is Cl–C(=O)–Cl. Remember: CCl4 does not burn, but when it falls on a flame it too forms the highly poisonous phosgene.

t: Chloroform Analysis: Six-Stage Order of Reactions
n: The analysis of chloroform is carried out in six stages. First: the distillate is heated with alcoholic alkali, and an AgCl precipitate is obtained with AgNO3 in a nitric acid medium; this reaction has negative significance. Second: the isonitrile reaction, a foul smell with aniline and alkali. Third: the resorcinol reaction, a red colour in alkaline solution. Fourth: Fujiwara, a red colour with pyridine and alkali. Fifth: Fehling's solution, a yellow and then a red precipitate. Sixth: quantitative determination by the argentometric method, the indicator being ferric ammonium alum.

Determination of organically bound chlorine. When the distillate is heated with an alcoholic alkali solution, chloride is formed. In a nitric acid medium with silver nitrate it gives a white precipitate, that is, AgCl. Chloral hydrate with alkali first converts to chloroform: CCl3CHO + NaOH → CHCl3 + HCOONa. Then chloroform with alcoholic alkali forms NaCl, and NaCl with AgNO3 gives AgCl.

On the significance of the organic chlorine reaction. This reaction has negative forensic chemical significance. All compounds containing a chlorine atom give this reaction. For this reason a positive result does not prove chloroform, whereas a negative result shows the absence of an organochlorine compound.

The isonitrile reaction. If aniline and alkali are added to the distillate and heated, an isonitrile with a characteristic foul smell is formed. In the reaction, chloroform, aniline and alkali give an isonitrile, 3 NaCl and water. Dichloroethane does not give this reaction; CCl4 and chloral hydrate do.

The resorcinol reaction. If an alkaline solution of resorcinol is added to the distillate and heated, a red colour forms. Chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride, formaldehyde and chloroform give this reaction; 1,2-dichloroethane does not. The sensitivity of the reaction is 3.0 mg of CHCl3.

The Fujiwara reaction. When pyridine is heated with alkyl halides on a water bath under alkaline conditions, a red colour forms. The pyridine salt in an alkaline medium converts to derivatives of glutaconic aldehyde. As a result of the reaction, a red polymethine dye is formed.

Reaction with Fehling's solution. Chloroform and chloral hydrate, when heated with Fehling's solutions 1 and 2, give first a yellow and then a red precipitate. CCl4 and dichloroethane do not give this reaction. CHCl3, chloral hydrate and formaldehyde, which have reducing properties, give this reaction. The sensitivity is 0.3 mg. CCl4 does not give it because in an alkaline medium it does not form a reducing agent such as HCOOH.

Quantitative determination. The quantity is determined by the argentometric method after separating the organically bound chlorine; the indicator is ferric ammonium alum. The chlorine-containing compound can also first be converted to inorganic chloride in the presence of sodium alcoholate and determined by the volumetric argentometric method. The quantity can also be determined by the GLC method.

Let us differentiate the results of the reactions according to the table. The isonitrile and Fehling reactions help to distinguish chloroform, chloral hydrate, CCl4 and dichloroethane. The isonitrile reaction is given by CHCl3, CCl4 and chloral hydrate, but not by DCE, that is, dichloroethane. The Fehling reaction is given by CHCl3 and chloral hydrate, not by CCl4 or DCE. Fujiwara gives a red colour with alkyl halides. DCE does not give the isonitrile and Fehling reactions; it is identified through copper acetylide and ethylene glycol, copper acetylide giving a pink or cherry-red colour.

t: Chloral Hydrate: Its Place in Medicine
n: Now chloral hydrate. It acts on the body like chloroform: first it excites the nervous system, then it calms it. In medicine, in a dose of about 0.2-0.5 g, it is used as a sedative and hypnotic preparation; the daily dose is 6 g; it is kept in Cabinet B. The maximum single dose is 2 g. It has also been used in mental agitation and to stop convulsions.

Chloral hydrate poisoning and metabolism. It has an adverse effect on the cardiovascular system: breathing quickens, body temperature falls, the pupils constrict. Death occurs from cessation of breathing and heartbeat. The lethal amount is not known; according to some scientists, about 10 g. The main metabolites: trichloroethanol and trichloroacetic acid.

t: Alkyl Halides: Comparison of Dangerous Amounts
n: Let us compare the dangerous amounts. Chloroform in the amount of 5-10 g leads to severe poisoning. Chloral hydrate in medicine 0.2-0.5 g, daily dose 6 g. For CCl4 the medicinal dose is 3 ml. 1,2-Dichloroethane in the amount of 15-20 ml leads to death.

t: Chloral Hydrate: Properties and Conversion to Chloroform
n: Properties of chloral hydrate. It is colourless, clear crystals or powder with a specific sharp odour and a bitter taste; it dissolves well in water and ether. In an alkaline medium and at high temperature it decomposes, forming chloroform: CCl3CHO + NaOH → CHCl3 + HCOONa. Because the reactions for identification from the distillate take place in a strongly alkaline medium, chloroform is formed quickly from chloral hydrate. For this reason the analytical reactions of the two are the same.

How do we distinguish chloroform and chloral hydrate? For this, an ether extract is obtained from the distillate in pure form. With Nessler's reagent, chloral hydrate gives a red-brown precipitate; if the precipitate stands, it turns dirty green. The quantity of chloral hydrate, like that of chloroform, is determined by GLC.

Now carbon tetrachloride. CCl4 has a toxic effect on the body; it is used for dissolving lacquers, oil paints and rubber, and for preserving skins and wool. In medicine and veterinary practice it is used as an anthelmintic, and also for extinguishing fires. The heavy vapour separates burning substances such as oil and petrol from atmospheric oxygen and extinguishes them.

CCl4 poisoning. It is rapidly absorbed into the body through mucous membranes; when used as a medicine, fatty food must not be eaten. The dose is 3 ml. In poisoning, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, dizziness and states of intoxication occur. It rapidly impairs the liver and kidneys, jaundice develops, and the liver undergoes fatty change; in poisoning through the respiratory tract, collapse is observed. CCl4 is kept in Cabinet B; workers at enterprises connected with it must undergo a medical examination every 6 months.

Properties and toxicology of CCl4. It is a heavy, clear, mobile liquid; it dissolves in water at 20 °C to about 0.01%, its boiling point is 75-77 °C, it distils easily with steam and does not burn. It has a narcotic effect and impairs the central nervous system; the lethal amount is 30-60 ml. Its metabolites are CHCl3 and CO2. The smallest amount that can be distilled over with water from 100 g of object is about 1 g.

Identity reactions of CCl4. In forensic chemical analysis, the identity of CCl4 is established by all the reactions given for CHCl3. It does not react with Fehling's solution; with 2,7-dihydroxynaphthalene it gives a light brown and then a greenish-yellow colour. To determine CCl4 in air, pyridine and aniline are allowed to act on the solution and it is heated, whereupon a red colour appears.

Now 1,2-dichloroethane, DCE for short. It differs from chloroform and CCl4 in burning with a smoky flame. Chemically pure DCE is a heavy, mobile liquid, similar in odour to chloroform, boiling at 83.7°. It is resistant to the action of acids and alkalis; it is almost insoluble in water and dissolves well in alcohol and ether. The isomer 1,1-dichloroethane is also a colourless liquid with a boiling point of 58 °C, but in industry 1,2-dichloroethane is mainly used.

Uses of dichloroethane. In enterprises it is used for dissolving fats, paints, resins and paraffins. In chemical laboratories it is used for extracting many organic substances, separating fats in wool, and cleaning clothing. It is one of the main raw materials for the synthesis of plastics and ion exchangers; it is also used in isolating alkaloids, and as an insecto-fungicide and antiseptic.

Dichloroethane poisoning. DCE enters the body through the respiratory tract. In poisoning, vomiting, diarrhoea, pain in the liver, abdominal distension and uraemia are observed. 15-20 ml of DCE leads to death; mutagenic and carcinogenic action has been established in the literature. The first symptoms are felt after 5-10 minutes; the vomit smells of dichloroethane; death may occur within two days. DCE is isolated from a biological object by steam distillation.

Heating DCE with alkali. When DCE is heated with alkali, the chlorine atom is not completely split off. The reaction: CH2Cl–CH2Cl + NaOH in alcoholic solution → NaCl + CHCl=CH2 + H2O. The chloride is determined with HNO3 and AgNO3.

t: DCE: The Ampoule Method and Ethylene Glycol
n: The ampoule method for DCE and ethylene glycol. As Nazarenko and Lapkina showed in 1952, chlorine is readily split off when heated under pressure in a bicarbonate or alkaline medium, that is, in a sealed ampoule. As a result, ethylene glycol is formed: ClCH2–CH2Cl + Na2CO3 + H2O → HO–CH2–CH2–OH + 2NaCl + CO2. This reaction is the basis of the method of determining DCE by forming ethylene glycol and then oxidising it to formaldehyde.

Obtaining formaldehyde from ethylene glycol. Ethylene glycol is oxidised to formaldehyde with KIO4 and H2SO4. The formaldehyde is determined with chromotropic acid or fuchsin-sulphurous acid. With these reagents, in the presence of mineral acids, formaldehyde forms a pink colour, that is, a quinoid compound. The sequence: DCE and Na2CO3 are heated in an ampoule, ethylene glycol is formed, it is oxidised to formaldehyde and gives a pink colour with fuchsin-sulphurous acid.

The copper acetylide reaction of DCE. DCE and sodium hydroxide are placed in an ampoule, which is sealed and boiled on a water bath. Acetylene is formed; with copper salts it gives pink or cherry-red copper acetylide. The reaction: ClCH2–CH2Cl + 2NaOH → HC≡CH + 2NaCl + 2H2O.

t: DCE: Reactions It Does Not Give and Additional Methods
n: Reactions that DCE does not give, and additional methods. DCE does not form an isonitrile and does not react with Fehling's solution. In the reaction with quinoline, a cyanine dye, a brown or red-brown colour, is formed. DCE can be determined by GLC; DCE in the atmosphere and in seed grain is transferred to an alcoholic solution and analysed.

The order of the identity analysis of 1,2-dichloroethane. In addition to the general reactions characteristic of alkyl halides, DCE gives specific reactions: Fujiwara and the determination of the chlorine atom. First, Fujiwara, a red colour with pyridine. Second, on heating with alkali the chlorine atom is not completely split off. Third, the ampoule method: with bicarbonate or alkali, ethylene glycol is formed, then formaldehyde. Fourth, forming acetylene and identifying it with copper acetylide. Fifth, DCE does not give the isonitrile and Fehling reactions.

General scheme of analysis. First, organically bound chlorine is determined; this reaction has negative significance. Then the isonitrile, Fehling, resorcinol and Fujiwara reactions are carried out. For dichloroethane, the copper acetylide and ethylene glycol → formaldehyde reactions are used. The result is confirmed by GLC; the quantity is determined by argentometry or GLC.

Conclusion. Alkyl halides distil with steam. The reaction for determining organically bound chlorine has negative significance, because all chlorine-containing compounds give it. By the results of the isonitrile, Fehling, resorcinol and Fujiwara reactions, chloroform, chloral hydrate, CCl4 and DCE are distinguished. DCE is distinguished through ethylene glycol, that is, the ampoule method, and copper acetylide, and chloral hydrate by its conversion to chloroform in alkali.
